## Loading packages

```{r packages, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
```

## Import dataset

```{r Reading Dataset, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
All_Country <- read_csv("Data/Processed/AllCountries_Processed.csv")
```

## Analysis

Linear regression model between "Electricity Bill Price" and "Outage Duration Hours" to see if the higher the electricity bill, the more stable the connection is.

```{r ggplot by country}
#Kenya
All_Country %>% 
  filter(Country == "Kenya") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = OutageDurationHours, y = ElectricityBillPriceUSD)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

#Liberia
All_Country %>% 
  filter(Country == "Liberia") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = OutageDurationHours, y = ElectricityBillPriceUSD)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

#Niger
All_Country %>% 
  filter(Country == "Niger") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = OutageDurationHours, y = ElectricityBillPriceUSD)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

#Rwanda
All_Country %>% 
  filter(Country == "Rwanda") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = OutageDurationHours, y = ElectricityBillPriceUSD)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

#Zambia
All_Country %>% 
  filter(Country == "Zambia") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = OutageDurationHours, y = ElectricityBillPriceUSD)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

Liberia is currently missing the values on Electricity bill price. Niger has some very large values on outage duration hours. Zambia somehow has some negative values on outage duration hours.

```{r ggplot all country}
All_Country %>% 
  filter(OutageDurationHours >= 0 & OutageDurationHours <= 168) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = OutageDurationHours, y = ElectricityBillPriceUSD)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_classic()
```

I removed the values larger than 168 hours in the outage duration hours column, because a week can only have 168 hours and any number larger than that is likely an error.

```{r Liner Regression Summary}
All_Country_Filtered <- All_Country %>%
  filter(OutageDurationHours >= 0 & OutageDurationHours <= 168)

LinearRegression <- lm(ElectricityBillPriceUSD ~ OutageDurationHours,
                       data = All_Country_Filtered)

summary(LinearRegression)
```
From the Linear Regression summary the R value is 0.01862, showing a very week positive correlation between Electricity Bill Price and Outage Duration Hours.






## Simple Linear Regression

For the NTL-LTER dataset, can we predict irradiance (light level) from depth?

```{r correlation}
# Correlation
cor.test(All_Country_Filtered$ElectricityBillPriceUSD, All_Country_Filtered$OutageDurationHours)
```

An exploratory option to visualize the model fit is to use the function `plot`. This function will return four graphs, which are intended only for checking the fit of the model and not for communicating results. The plots that are returned are: 

1. **Residuals vs. Fitted.** The value predicted by the line of best fit is the fitted value, and the residual is the distance of that actual value from the predicted value. By definition, there will be a balance of positive and negative residuals. Watch for drastic asymmetry from side to side or a marked departure from zero for the red line - these are signs of a poor model fit.

2. **Normal Q-Q.** The points should fall close to the 1:1 line. We often see departures from 1:1 at the high and low ends of the dataset, which could be outliers. 

3. **Scale-Location.** Similar to the residuals vs. fitted graph, this will graph the squared standardized residuals by the fitted values. 

4. **Residuals vs. Leverage.** This graph will display potential outliers. The values that fall outside the dashed red lines (Cook's distance) are outliers for the model. Watch for drastic departures of the solid red line from horizontal - this is a sign of a poor model fit.

## Testing distribution

```{r, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 4}
par(mfrow = c(2,2), mar=c(2,2,2,1))
plot(LinearRegression)
```

##log transforming and testing distribution again

```{r log transform, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 4}
LogRegression <- lm(log(ElectricityBillPriceUSD + 1) ~ log(OutageDurationHours + 1), data = All_Country_Filtered)
summary(LogRegression)

par(mfrow = c(2,2), mar=c(2,2,2,1))
plot(LogRegression)
par(mfrow = c(1,1))
```

## Plotting the log transformed graph

```{r, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 4}
# Add a line and standard error for the linear regression
LogCountryPlot <- 
  ggplot(All_Country_Filtered, aes(x = log1p(OutageDurationHours), y = log1p(ElectricityBillPriceUSD))) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  geom_point() +
  theme_classic()

print(LogCountryPlot) 
```
